paras: The threatened lynching of Sam Johnson occurred in Colusa and Yolo counties, California, in August 1915, when posses and crowds of ranchers threatened to lynch Johnson, a Black man accused of fatally shooting Richard Lindsay and attacking Lindsay's aunt, Mrs. Michael Blevins. A member of the searching party fired four shots at Johnson before his capture near Capay on August 3, and a crowd gathered at the Woodland depot to meet his train. The Colusa County sheriff evaded a mob by driving Johnson to the jail at Marysville, and a month later the accused, there named "Sam Robertson," was reported to have pleaded guilty and been sentenced to hang.

According to an Associated Press dispatch, Johnson, discharged from a wood-chopping job, went to the Blevins ranch near Arbuckle while the sheepman was away, and Mrs. Blevins kept him off until her nephew arrived. The dispatch said Johnson shot Lindsay with a shotgun on Sunday night, August 1, and fled when Mrs. Blevins fired a rifle at him. The Associated Press called the shooting "alleged," while United Press dispatches stated as fact that he had "attacked" Mrs. Blevins and "murdered" her nephew.

On August 2 the sheriffs of Colusa, Glenn and Yolo counties led posses with bloodhounds through the foothills west of Arbuckle, and the Associated Press reported "talk of a lynching if Johnson is caught." Lindsay died at St. Francis hospital in San Francisco at 2 a.m. on August 3; when the posses learned of his death the search went on "with renewed vigor," and talk of lynching was "frequently heard."

That afternoon Johnson was found along a creek near Capay, west of Woodland. In the version printed by the Salem Daily Capital Journal, Jack Woods, "a young farmer who was a member of the mob searching for the negro," fired at him four times "in an effort to cripple him," missing each time, before Johnson surrendered. Sheriff Stanton's posse then arrived and took him, and the sheriff quieted the "gang of ranchers" who threatened to lynch him.

Told that the train carrying Johnson to Colusa would pass through Woodland, a crowd swarmed the depot platform, "prepared to mob the negro if they got a chance," but the train did not stop. According to a Sacramento dispatch the next day, Stanton did not take his prisoner to Colusa "because a mob had gathered with Blevens, husband of the woman, as ring leader," and instead drove him by automobile from Woodland to the Yuba County jail at Marysville.

He was to stay there "until the excitement dies down" and then be moved secretly to Colusa. No report of arrests among the posses or crowds was found. On September 4 a Colusa dispatch reported that "Sam Robertson, negro," who had killed Richard Lindsey on the Blevins ranch on August 1, had pleaded guilty and was sentenced to hang after Mrs. Blevins testified.

White papers in Iowa, Wisconsin, Arizona, Nevada, Oregon and southern California ran brief wire dispatches on August 3 and 4. Their headlines led with the mob, "Lynch Talk is Heard," "May Lynch Negro in California," "California Mob May Hang Negro," "Sheriff Fearful of Party of Lynchers," or with the hunt, "Search for Negro" and "After Black Fiend." United Press copy called Johnson a "culprit" and "the negro fiend" and reported the threats without comment.

The Oakland Sunshine, a Black weekly, took up the case on August 7 in its society column. It wrote that "it seems as though" a colored man named Samuel Johnson had killed a white boy and attacked his aunt, but faulted the Yolo Democrat for omitting what "the other papers stated," that Johnson had been confined in two insane asylums. "We do not believe the Negro is now rational," the Sunshine concluded; it did not mention the lynching threats.

Reports differed on the accused's name: most called him Sam Johnson, an Associated Press dispatch of August 4 called him "William Johnson," and the September sentencing report named him "Sam Robertson." The Elko Independent called Woods "a member of the sheriff's posse," the Capital Journal a member of "the mob." The Tonopah Daily Bonanza dated the killing August 2, against August 1 in the sentencing report.

bases: Posses and crowds of ranchers threatened to lynch Johnson, a posse member fired four shots at him, and a crowd waited at the Woodland depot, but the sheriff kept him and no one was killed by the mob (A3, A7, A10).

accounts.gist: Johnson, discharged from wood-chopping, went to the Blevins ranch; he is 'alleged' to have shot Lindsay with a shotgun; Mrs. Blevins drove him off with a rifle; talk of lynching if he is caught.

accounts.label: United Press capture report (Woodland, Aug. 3)
accounts.gist: Johnson, who 'attacked' Mrs. Blevins and 'murdered' Lindsay, was captured near Capay after Jack Woods fired four shots; a crowd waited at the Woodland depot; ranchers threatened lynching until the sheriff quieted them.

accounts.label: Sacramento dispatch (Aug. 4)
accounts.gist: Sheriff Stanton, fearing a mob led by Blevins at Colusa, drove the prisoner to the Marysville jail.

accounts.label: Black weekly (Oakland Sunshine)
accounts.gist: Accepts that Johnson killed Lindsay and attacked his aunt, but says he had been in two insane asylums in Tennessee and was not rational.

accounts.label: Colusa sentencing report (Sept. 4)
accounts.gist: 'Sam Robertson' pleaded guilty to killing Lindsey before attacking Mrs. Blevins on Aug. 1 and was sentenced to hang.

framing.detail: AP dispatches under 'Search for Negro' and 'After Black Fiend' called the shooting 'alleged' and reported lynching talk without comment.
UP reports headed 'May Lynch Negro' and 'California Mob May Hang Negro' called Johnson 'the negro fiend' and a 'culprit' and stated the accusation as fact, while reporting the mob threat neutrally.
The Oakland Sunshine accepted the accusation but argued the man was insane and faulted the Yolo Democrat for omitting his asylum history; it said nothing of the lynching threats.

conflicts.note: The September report matches the victims, ranch and date, so it is very likely the same man under another name; no report explains the difference.
